# Speech and Realtime Voice {#sec-speech}

Speech is a timed signal: words arrive inside a voice, listeners respond before
every sentence is complete, and two people may speak at once. A batch
transcription system can wait for the recording to end. A live captioner must
revise its partial hypotheses, the provisional transcript of speech still in
progress, without distracting the reader. A voice assistant must also detect when
the user has finished speaking (endpointing), begin producing audio, and keep
listening while it speaks. Streaming changes what counts as correct.

This chapter develops the stack in that order. It begins with the latent alignment
between audio frames and text, then explains how learned representations and
neural codecs reduce the amount of audio a model must process. It closes with
speech generation and with the requirements that a usable conversation places on
every layer.

## Treat speech as a timed stream

A speech system first converts the waveform into a sequence of short, overlapping
frames. What happens next depends on the application:

| Workload | May use future audio? | First useful output | Main failure to measure |
|---|---:|---|---|
| Recorded transcription | Yes | Complete transcript | Word errors |
| Live captions | Limited look-ahead | Stable partial text | Revisions and delay |
| Turn-based voice assistant | Until end of turn | First reply audio | Late or false endpoint |
| Full-duplex conversation | No fixed turn boundary | Speech, pause, or interruption response | Overlap and state errors |

Each workload needs its own measurement. A model can have an excellent final
transcript while its partial text changes too often for captions. A synthesizer
can render natural speech faster than real time yet take too long to produce its
first audio frame. A claim that a system is “realtime” therefore has to name the
measurement it refers to.

## Learn an alignment for recognition

@gls-asr observes acoustic frames
$\mathbf{x}=(x_1,\ldots,x_T)$ and a shorter transcript
$\mathbf{y}=(y_1,\ldots,y_U)$, but no label says which frames produced each
symbol. @gls-ctc and the recurrent neural network transducer (RNN-T) treat that
alignment as a latent, unobserved variable and sum over every monotonic
alignment, meaning every assignment of frames to symbols that preserves
transcript order. An attention-based encoder-decoder instead learns a soft
correspondence between encoder frames and output steps.

@gls-ctc adds a blank symbol and assigns probability to every length-$T$ path
that collapses to the transcript [@graves2006ctc]:

$$
p_{\mathrm{CTC}}(\mathbf{y}\mid\mathbf{x})
=
\sum_{\boldsymbol{\pi}\in B^{-1}(\mathbf{y})}
\prod_{t=1}^{T}p(\pi_t\mid\mathbf{x}).
$$

Here $\boldsymbol{\pi}$ is a path over the output alphabet plus blank, and
$B$ merges consecutive repeated labels and removes blanks. A forward-backward
dynamic program evaluates the sum without enumerating every path. Standard CTC
factorizes the path emissions across frames, conditioned on the encoder output.
It has no explicit label-history model, although a contextual encoder can still
use broad acoustic context and an external language model remains optional.

RNN-T adds output history [@graves2012rnnt]. Its prediction network summarizes
preceding nonblank labels, and its joint network combines that state with an
acoustic encoder state. In the alignment lattice, blank advances acoustic time;
a label advances output position. The model may therefore emit several labels at
one encoder step. A causal encoder, which reads only past and current frames, or a
bounded-context encoder makes this factorization suitable for online decoding,
but RNN-T by itself does not guarantee streaming.
The original model used a bidirectional transcription network, while later work
demonstrated a causal on-device system [@he2019streaming].

An attention-based encoder-decoder such as Listen, Attend and Spell models

$$
p(\mathbf{y}\mid\mathbf{x})
=\prod_{u=1}^{U}p(y_u\mid y_{<u},c_u),
\qquad
c_u=\sum_t\alpha_{u,t}h_t,
$$

where $h_t$ is an encoder state and $\alpha_{u,t}$ is its attention weight
at output step $u$ [@chan2016las]. The original system could attend over the
whole utterance, so it was offline. Monotonic, chunked, or limited-look-ahead
attention can trade future context for lower delay.

These alignment objectives can sit on several encoder families. Conformer is an
encoder architecture, not an alignment objective. Each Conformer block combines
convolution for local acoustic patterns with self-attention for longer-range
interactions [@gulati2020conformer]. Its original full-context attention was also
offline; streaming implementations constrain that context.

## Pretrain representations before transcribing

Transcripts are expensive, while raw audio is plentiful. Self-supervision and weak
supervision solve different data problems: self-supervision derives its training
targets from untranscribed audio, and weak supervision trains on abundant but
noisy transcripts.

| Method | Training signal | What the model predicts |
|---|---|---|
| wav2vec 2.0 | Untranscribed audio | A masked step's quantized target among distractors |
| HuBERT | Untranscribed audio plus offline clusters | Cluster labels at masked positions |
| WavLM | Clean speech targets with corrupted or overlapped input | Primary-speech cluster labels |
| Whisper | Audio paired with noisy human or machine text | Text, language, task, and timestamp tokens |

wav2vec 2.0 masks spans in a latent sequence. At each masked position $t$, its
context vector $c_t$ must distinguish the corresponding quantized target
$q_t$ from a set $Q_t$ containing that target and distractors
[@baevski2020wav2vec2]:

$$
\mathcal{L}_t=-\log
\frac{\exp(\operatorname{sim}(c_t,q_t)/\kappa)}
{\sum_{\widetilde q\in Q_t}
\exp(\operatorname{sim}(c_t,\widetilde q)/\kappa)}.
$$

Here, the similarity is cosine similarity and $\kappa$ is a temperature. The
targets are the masked steps themselves, not future continuations. In one reported
low-resource setting, a large model pretrained on 53,000 hours of Libri-Light and
fine-tuned on ten labeled minutes reached 4.8 and 8.2 word error rate on
LibriSpeech test-clean and test-other; that result also used a Transformer
language model during decoding.

HuBERT replaces contrastive selection with masked prediction of offline cluster
assignments, labels produced by clustering audio features before training
[@hsu2021hubert]. It begins with clusters of handcrafted features, then can
recluster representations produced by an earlier training stage. The targets stay
fixed within a stage. The paper found that consistent targets can be useful even
when they are imperfect phonetic labels.
WavLM keeps this masked pseudo-label objective but sometimes adds noise or another
speaker to the input. Its target remains the cluster label from the original
primary utterance, so it learns to identify content through interference rather
than reconstructing a clean waveform [@chen2022wavlm].

Whisper follows a different recipe: 680,000 hours of weakly supervised,
multilingual audio-text pairs train one encoder-decoder Transformer
[@radford2022whisper]. Its decoder sequence carries a language token, a
transcription-or-translation task token, controls for timestamps, and the text;
when enabled, timestamp tokens are interleaved around transcript spans. The main
result is broad zero-shot transfer: accuracy across held-out datasets that the
model was never fine-tuned on. It does not establish universal superiority to a
system tuned for one domain.

## Turn waveforms into codec indices

A neural codec compresses a waveform into discrete indices. An encoder maps audio
to one latent vector $z_t$ per frame, a quantizer replaces each vector with
entries from a codebook, a learned table of vectors, and a decoder reconstructs
audio. SoundStream established an end-to-end residual-vector-quantized design with
quantizer dropout, which trains with a randomly chosen number of quantizers so
that one model serves multiple bitrates [@zeghidour2021soundstream]. EnCodec
combined a streaming encoder-decoder, residual vector quantization, adversarial
training, and optional entropy coding [@defossez2022encodec]. Their quality claims are tied to the
bitrates, datasets, and listening tests reported in those papers.

Residual vector quantization (RVQ) applies codebooks in sequence. For frame $t$,
let $r_t^{(0)}=z_t$. At depth $j$, choose the nearest entry and pass on the
unexplained residual:

$$
k_t^{(j)}=\arg\min_k\left\lVert r_t^{(j-1)}-e_k^{(j)}\right\rVert_2^2,
\qquad
r_t^{(j)}=r_t^{(j-1)}-e_{k_t^{(j)}}^{(j)},
\qquad
\widehat z_t=\sum_{j=1}^{Q}e_{k_t^{(j)}}^{(j)}.
$$

Here $e_k^{(j)}$ is entry $k$ in codebook $j$, $k_t^{(j)}$ is its index,
and $Q$ is the active depth. Later codebooks refine what earlier ones missed.
This usually improves reconstruction, but it also sends more indices.

If the codec emits $f$ frames per second and uses $Q$ codebooks, its raw index
traffic is

$$
R_{\mathrm{idx}}=fQ.
$$

If codebook $j$ contains $K_j$ entries and each index uses a fixed-width
integer, the nominal payload is

$$
R_{\mathrm{bit}}=f\sum_{j=1}^{Q}\left\lceil\log_2K_j\right\rceil.
$$

Token rate is not bitrate. Neither number alone gives a generator's decoding
cost: a model may predict codebooks sequentially, in parallel, or in groups.

```{figure}
//| figure: residual-vq
//| label: fig-speech-and-voice-1
//| fig-cap: "Residual vector quantization of one two-dimensional frame, with three hand-set four-entry codebooks at 50 frames per second. Each panel is one codebook, drawn in residual coordinates at its own scale: the cross is the residual the stage must explain, hollow circles are the codebook's entries with their indices, the filled circle is the nearest entry, whose index the stage sends, the dashed circle through it shows that every other entry lies farther away, and the arrow from that entry to the cross is the new residual passed to the next codebook. Panels beyond the active depth $Q$ are dimmed, and the readout gives $\widehat z$ with the rates $R_{\mathrm{idx}}=fQ$ and $R_{\mathrm{bit}}=f\sum_{j}\lceil\log_2K_j\rceil$. The frames include one that later codebooks refine more slowly and frames the small codebooks barely reach, where a stage sends the zero entry and removes no error. The codebooks are hand-set values, not a trained codec; the runnable below trains them."
depth: 2
frame: a
```

The runnable below trains the codebooks instead of setting them by hand. On
4,000 two-dimensional unit-Gaussian frames it fits eight residual stages of
four entries each with k-means, each stage on the residuals the earlier stages
leave, and measures the error on 4,000 held-out frames against the bits per
frame $\sum_j\lceil\log_2K_j\rceil$. It compares one flat codebook of $2^b$
entries at the same $b$ bits, trained the same way, and the distortion-rate
function $D(R)=2^{-2R/d}$ of a unit Gaussian, the lowest error any code can
reach at $R$ bits per $d$-dimensional frame. The cell asserts that every stage
lowers the error, that no code falls below the bound, and that up to 6 bits the
flat codebook is at least as accurate as the residual stages. The labels count
stored entries: residual stages grow linearly, 32 at 16 bits, where one flat
codebook would need 65,536, which is why codecs stack small codebooks. The
price is a gap to the bound that widens with depth. Set `K = 16` and `Q = 4`:
the same 16 bits per frame from fewer, larger stages cut the error about
threefold.

:::: {.runnable}
```python
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
d, K, Q, frame_hz = 2, 4, 8, 50              # frame dimension, entries per codebook, depth, rate
train, test = rng.normal(size=(4000, d)), rng.normal(size=(4000, d))   # unit-variance frames

def kmeans(x, k, iters=30):
    c = x[rng.choice(len(x), k, replace=False)]
    for _ in range(iters):
        a = ((x[:, None] - c) ** 2).sum(-1).argmin(1)
        n = np.bincount(a, minlength=k)
        s = np.zeros_like(c); np.add.at(s, a, x)
        c = np.where(n[:, None] > 0, s / np.maximum(n, 1)[:, None], c)
    return c

def quantize(x, c):
    return c[((x[:, None] - c) ** 2).sum(-1).argmin(1)]

rvq, r_train, r_test = [], train.copy(), test.copy()
for q in range(Q):                           # each stage learns what earlier stages left over
    c = kmeans(r_train, K)
    r_train -= quantize(r_train, c)
    r_test -= quantize(r_test, c)
    rvq.append((r_test ** 2).mean())         # held-out squared error per dimension
bits = np.arange(1, Q + 1) * np.ceil(np.log2(K))   # bits per frame, sum of ceil(log2 K_j)
flat = [((test - quantize(test, kmeans(train, 2 ** int(b)))) ** 2).mean() for b in bits[bits <= 6]]
bound = 2.0 ** (-2 * bits / d)               # distortion-rate function of a unit Gaussian
assert np.all(np.diff(rvq) < 0) and np.all(np.array(rvq) > bound)
assert np.all(np.array(flat) <= np.array(rvq[:len(flat)]) * 1.02)   # one big codebook is better

plt.figure(figsize=(5.6, 4.0))
plt.semilogy(bits, rvq, "o-", ms=4, label=f"residual VQ, {K} entries per stage")
plt.semilogy(bits[:len(flat)], flat, "s", ms=5, label="one codebook of 2^bits entries")
plt.semilogy(bits, bound, "--", color="gray", lw=1, label="D(R), Gaussian bound")
for b, e, q in zip(bits[1::2], rvq[1::2], range(2, Q + 1, 2)):   # codebook entries stored
    plt.annotate(f"{K * q} vs {2 ** int(b):,}" + " entries" * (q == 2), (b, e),
                 textcoords="offset points", xytext=(4, 6), fontsize=8)
plt.xlabel(f"bits per frame (bit/s = {frame_hz} x bits)")
plt.ylabel("squared error per dimension")
plt.title("Residual stages: few entries, a growing gap to the bound")
plt.legend(fontsize=9, loc="lower left")
print(f"depth {Q}: {bits[-1]:.0f} bits/frame = {bits[-1] * frame_hz:.0f} bit/s, "
      f"error {rvq[-1]:.2e}, {rvq[-1] / bound[-1]:.1f}x the bound")
```
::::

“Semantic” and “acoustic” are roles, not a clean partition. Tokens from a
self-supervised speech model tend to preserve linguistic content while discarding
some speaker and recording detail. Codec tokens must preserve enough information
to reconstruct the signal, so they also carry content. Systems can encourage a
division: SpeechTokenizer distills its first RVQ layer toward HuBERT units, the
cluster labels described above [@zhang2024speechtokenizer], while later layers
refine the audio. AudioLM uses
w2v-BERT units for long-range structure and SoundStream codes for fidelity
[@chung2021w2vbert; @borsos2022audiolm]. The Descript Audio Codec targets
high-fidelity 44.1 kHz audio with improved quantizer use [@kumar2023dac]. Mimi,
the codec of the Moshi conversation model discussed later in this chapter,
operates at 12.5 frames per second and combines a semantic
quantizer with acoustic RVQ levels [@defossez2024moshi]. A low frame rate shortens
the time axis, but quality, codebook depth, and the generator's schedule still
determine the actual cost.

## Choose a generation representation and schedule

AudioLM first models semantic units, then coarse and fine acoustic tokens. This
hierarchy gave its samples longer-range coherence without asking one flat codec
model to learn every timescale at once [@borsos2022audiolm]. @gls-tts, the task of
synthesizing speech from text, adds a transcript and often a short acoustic prompt
that identifies the target voice.

VALL-E predicts EnCodec tokens conditioned on text and a three-second enrollment
recording of the target speaker. Its autoregressive stage produces the first
codebook, and its non-autoregressive stage fills residual codebooks one level at
a time, with frame positions parallel within a level [@wang2023valle]. SoundStorm
uses confidence-based masked decoding across positions; in the authors' TPU-v4
setup, it generated thirty seconds of audio in half a second
[@borsos2023soundstorm]. VALL-E 2 changed
codec grouping and sampling to reduce repetition. Its “human parity” claim refers
to the paper's preference tests on LibriSpeech and VCTK, not to every speaker,
language, or recording condition [@chen2024valle2].

Continuous generators offer another path. Voicebox works on the mel-spectrogram,
a time-frequency picture of audio with frequencies on a perceptual scale. It uses
conditional flow matching, a training method that learns to transform noise into
data given a conditioning input, to infill masked spectrogram spans, enabling
synthesis, editing, denoising, and style transfer in one model [@le2023voicebox].
NaturalSpeech 3 instead factorizes speech into content, prosody (rhythm, stress,
and intonation), speaker identity, and acoustic detail, then uses discrete masked
diffusion for the generated factors [@ju2024naturalspeech3]. F5-TTS removes an explicit alignment search and duration
predictor from training, but inference still needs a target duration to define the
generated span [@chen2024f5tts].

| Representation and schedule | Useful property | Design constraint |
|---|---|---|
| Autoregressive codec tokens | Natural variable-length generation | Serial dependencies can repeat or drift |
| Masked codec tokens | Many frame positions update together | Several refinement passes may be required |
| Flow or diffusion over spectrograms | Global conditioning and editing | Sampling schedule and output length must be chosen |

None of these rows guarantees or forbids streaming. Chunking, causal context,
look-ahead, and the vocoder, the component that turns generated spectrograms or
tokens into a waveform, determine when audio can leave the system.

Voice cloning also makes consent and provenance part of the technical design.
AudioSeal jointly trains a watermark generator and a detector that can localize
its embedded signal [@sanroman2024audioseal]. It is proactive rather than a
universal detector: the watermark must be embedded when the audio is generated,
and the detector recognizes content that carries it. It cannot prove that an
unmarked recording is human-made.

## Build conversation on incremental state

A turn-based cascade connects ASR, a text model, and TTS. Its components are easy
to inspect and replace, and text offers a useful control boundary. It can also
lose timing, overlap, pronunciation, and emotion unless those signals travel on
separate channels. Direct speech-to-speech models preserve more of the signal but
are harder to steer and diagnose.

For a purely serial cascade, time to first audio can be decomposed as

$$
D_{\mathrm{first}}=D_{\mathrm{endpoint}}+D_{\mathrm{in}}+D_{\mathrm{ASR}}
+D_{\mathrm{model}}+D_{\mathrm{TTS}}+D_{\mathrm{out}}.
$$

The terms cover endpoint detection, inbound transport, recognition, response
generation, synthesis, and outbound transport. Real systems overlap work, so the
observed delay follows the critical path rather than always equaling this serial
sum. Report time to first audio together with the endpoint rule and network
conditions. Real-time factor, total generation time divided by audio duration,
answers a different question.

```{figure}
//| figure: voice-first-audio
//| label: fig-voice-cascade-vs-e2e
//| fig-cap: "Time to first audio as a latency budget on one time axis, starting when the user stops speaking. Each stage row is one term of the decomposition $D_{\mathrm{first}}$ above: solid bars lie on the critical path to the first reply audio, faded bars are work that continues off it, and the hatched bar is the endpointer waiting for silence. Without streaming, each cascade stage waits for the previous one to finish, so the delay is the serial sum of whole-stage times. With streaming, ASR has processed most of the utterance while the user spoke, the text model hands its first phrase to TTS, and TTS sends its first chunk, so only the first-piece times add up along the critical path. The speech-to-speech model keeps audio inside one learned path; in full duplex it predicts the end of the turn itself instead of waiting for a silence timeout. Stage costs are illustrative, for a 2-second utterance and a 50-token reply. The audio model's 160 ms is the theoretical latency reported for Moshi, and the shaded band is the range of median human response offsets reported across ten languages."
streaming: true
duplex: false
endpoint: 500
network: 40
```

Full duplex is a systems contract: capture and input processing continue while
reply audio plays. That contract needs acoustic echo cancellation so the agent
does not hear itself, voice-activity and endpoint logic, interruption detection,
output cancellation, and a policy for rolling back text or tool actions produced
after the user barges in. Backchannels such as “mm-hm” are outputs too; they must
not accidentally claim a turn or trigger an action.

Moshi demonstrates one model-level implementation. It represents user and system
audio as parallel streams and predicts a text “inner monologue” before the system
audio at each step. The paper reports 160 ms theoretical latency and about 200 ms
in its practical setup [@defossez2024moshi]. These figures describe that system.

Human conversation is not a 200 ms service-level objective. Across ten languages,
Stivers and colleagues observed response-time distributions with modes from 0 to
200 ms and median offsets from 0 to 300 ms, with substantial variation by language
and response type [@stivers2009turntaking]. People also use pauses as meaningful
signals. A voice product should measure its own task: dictation, translation,
customer support, tutoring, and casual conversation tolerate different delays.

End-to-end audio products provide useful system evidence but limited architectural
detail. OpenAI reported 232 ms minimum and 320 ms average response time for GPT-4o
audio, and described one network trained across audio, vision, and text
[@openai2024gpt4o]. That does not by itself establish full-duplex behavior. Speech
translation is another neighboring workload: SeamlessM4T covers speech and text
translation and recognition across up to one hundred languages, with coverage
varying by task and direction [@seamless2023]. Seamless Streaming uses monotonic
attention for simultaneous translation; the same work also presents an expressive
speech-to-speech model [@seamless2023streaming].

## Benchmark every boundary

An end-to-end score cannot explain which layer failed. Keep boundary metrics beside
task-level listening tests:

| Boundary | Measures that answer the engineering question |
|---|---|
| Recognition | Word error rate, partial-hypothesis stability, emission delay |
| Codec | Listening quality at a named bitrate, algorithmic delay, robustness to packet loss |
| TTS | Intelligibility, speaker similarity, naturalness, real-time factor, time to first audio |
| Conversation | Endpoint errors, interruption response, overlap handling, echo leakage, tool-cancellation correctness |
| Safety | Speaker consent, impersonation tests, watermark survival and false alarms, retention of voice data |

For a reference transcript containing $N$ words, word error rate is

$$
\mathrm{WER}=\frac{S+D+I}{N},
$$

where $S$, $D$, and $I$ count substitutions, deletions, and insertions.
WER does not measure punctuation, speaker attribution, prosody, naturalness, or
whether a partial transcript arrived in time. Those need separate tests.

::: {.callout-important}
## What's contested
There is no generally best boundary between speech and text. A cascade exposes
transcripts, policy checks, and replaceable components. An end-to-end audio model
can retain timing and prosody and may overlap more computation, but its mistakes
are harder to attribute. Generation has the same unresolved choice between
autoregressive, masked, and continuous schedules. Select from measured workload
requirements rather than from an architecture label.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Lower-layer constraint
Conversation requirements reach every layer. An interruption target constrains
audio chunk size, endpointing, transport, model scheduling, synthesis buffering,
and cancellation. A codec's frame rate and codebook layout constrain how many
indices a generator must handle, but they do not determine latency alone. Write
the interaction contract first, then assign a measurable budget to each boundary.
:::
